notes.meaning: David had made up his mind to watch how he lived, and most of all what he said. He would keep a muzzle on his mouth, like a muzzle on a dog, while wicked people were around. He feared they would grab any grumbling from him and use it to mock God. The title hands the song to Jeduthun, one of David's chief temple singers.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine took the name Jeduthun to mean "leaping over them." To him it pictures any believer who rises above people whose hearts are set on passing earthly things.

notes.meaning: So David went completely quiet. He held back even good words, maybe afraid that something wrong would slip out once he started. But keeping it all inside did not ease his pain. It stirred his sorrow up even more. Several writers think he went too far here, because God also wants us to speak good and helpful words.

His feelings were like a fire that had been covered over. The longer he brooded on his troubles and on how well the wicked were doing, the hotter it burned. At last he could not hold it in, and he spoke. Many teachers see this as an honest confession that he broke out in complaint, even though he had meant to stay calm.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe David did not break his good promise here. He only stopped holding back good words, and the first thing he said was a prayer.

notes.meaning: It is good that he spoke to God and not to people. He asked God to help him truly grasp how short life is and how frail he is. He was not asking for the date of his death, which God keeps hidden. He wanted the wisdom to live ready for death.

differ.view: Some evangelicals read this as a tired, impatient wish. David was weary of suffering and wanted to know how long he had left to bear it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine took "my end" to mean the goal not yet reached. It is the prize Paul pressed toward, beyond this life of trials.

notes.meaning: A handbreadth is the width of four fingers. It was one of the smallest measures people used. God has made our lives that short, and next to his never-ending life they are as nothing. Even a person at his strongest and richest is only a breath. "Selah" seems to be a pause mark, telling us to stop and think about this.

People walk around like shadows, with only the look of a real life. They rush and make a lot of noise over things that come to nothing. They pile up money, yet they do not know who will end up with it after they die.
"And now" marks a turning point. If life and its riches are so empty, what is David waiting for? Nothing from this world. His hope rests on God alone, who lasts when everything else fails.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe David did not yet have a clear hope of life after death. Even facing death, he simply threw himself on the living God.

notes.meaning: Before asking for his pain to end, David asks to be set free from all his sins. He means their guilt, their punishment and their hold on him. He also asks not to become a joke to "fools." These are the godless people who love to laugh at believers when they fall.

Now David is quiet again, but it is a better kind of quiet. It is not sulking. It is humble trust. His trouble did not come by chance. It came from God's hand, so he will not argue or grumble against it.

Accepting God's will does not stop David from praying for relief. The only one who sent the blow can take it away, so he asks God to remove it. He is worn out, like a fighter who can go no longer and begs for mercy.

David turns his own case into a truth about everyone. When God corrects people for their sin, he eats away what they hold dear, the way a moth slowly ruins cloth. Beauty, health and strength all fade. Truly every person is only a breath.

His pleading grows stronger: first a prayer, then a cry, then tears. He reminds God that he is only a guest passing through the earth, just as his forefathers were. This world is not his true home. That is one more reason to ask for God's kindness, since God cares for strangers.

David asks God to turn his angry look away, so that he can smile again before he dies. Many read it as a godly request for more time. He wants to get his strength back and be ready before he leaves this world.

differ.view: Some evangelicals see these words as partly coming from deep sorrow that went too far. It shows how hard it is for believers to keep their words measured when death seems close.
